title: Nels G. Johnson, PhD
text:
An introduction
I am an R&D mathematical statistician working on scientific problems related to all things forest management. The data is often multivariate and longitudinal in space/time, and expensive to collect (i.e., time, labor, resources). It comes from many kinds of studies—designed experiments, observational surveys, and surveys of convenience and opportunity. As such, my work requires broad statistical expertise to meet the needs of many projects and partners.


The work I do
Most projects involves bread-and-butter statistical and machine learning techniques like generalized linear mixed models, decision trees, and random forests. These are powerful tools that are well understood and perform well when data is small or of modest size.
For the most complex projects I use Bayesian variants of models found in statistical physics (e.g., the Ising model). Their interpretation can be done in terms of simple physical systems like circuits and magnets.
For more information, see my portfolio.


My training
Before working in forest management R&D, I received my PhD in statistics from Virginia Tech and had postdoctoral fellowships in statistical ecology at Colorado State University and NIMBioS (now NIMBioS). As a graduate student, my assistantship was funded by working as a lead statistical collaborator at LISA (now SAIG). I also received an NSF Math-Bio Undergraduate Fellowship as an undergraduate mathematics student at UNCG.
For more information, see my CV.

title: CV
text:
I am a statistician and scientist with more than ten years of experience working on real research problems in ecology, forestry, and wildfire science. My work focuses on building statistical and machine-learning models that people can actually use to make decisions.
Much of this work involves Bayesian modeling, spatial data, and situations where data are messy, incomplete, or structured in ways that violate standard assumptions. I spend a large portion of my time collaborating with other scientists to design studies, choose appropriate models, and interpret results correctly.

title: CV
text:
Professional Experience

USDA Forest Service — Mathematical Statistician
2016 – Present

Built statistical and machine-learning models to study wildfire-related survival outcomes, which have been used in policy discussions and external guidance.
Developed probabilistic and nonlinear models to predict forest growth and support timber and land management decisions.
Designed models to support ecosystem restoration, including work on forest disease and recovery.
Advised more than 50 interdisciplinary research teams on study design, modeling approaches, and interpretation of results.
Trained and mentored more than 100 scientists through workshops, short courses, and one-on-one consultation in Bayesian modeling and applied statistics.



National Institute for Mathematical and Biological Synthesis (NIMBioS) — Postdoctoral Fellow
2015 – 2016

Developed Bayesian methods to study functional similarity in ecological systems.
Built clustering models for complex, multi-species data.
Worked closely with domain scientists to align statistical assumptions with biology.



Colorado State University — Postdoctoral Fellow
2013 – 2015

Developed Bayesian correction models for high-throughput sequencing data.
Produced spatial statistical analyses of soil microbial processes across large regions.
Collaborated across statistics, ecology, and biogeochemistry.



Virginia Tech — Laboratory for Interdisciplinary Statistical Analysis (LISA)
Lead Collaborator
2008 – 2013

Served as the primary statistical collaborator on more than 140 research projects.
Helped researchers design studies, analyze data, and prepare results for publication.
Taught short courses and workshops on applied statistical methods.

title: Research Scientist Knowledge
text:
Amazon’s research scientist interview prep guide has a nice overview of what they would like their research scientists to know. I thought it was a super cool and quite comprehensive list. It inspired me to make an inventory of all the knowledge I believe I have according to a personally defined taxonomy.

Supervised Learning Topics
Generalized linear mixed models, nonlinear mixed models, decision trees, random forests, gradient boosted models, Gaussian processes, point processes


Unsupervised Learning Topics
k-means, Gaussian mixture models


Probabilistic Graphical Models
Bayesian network, Markov networks, Markov chains, Monte Carlo methods, Gibbs-type algorithms.


Dimensionality Reduction
principal component analysis, singular value decomposition, multidimensional scaling


Sequential Models
multi-state models, hidden Markov models, conditional random fields, Makr


Training and Optimization
regularization, under fitting, over fitting, loss functions, Bayesian estimators, maximum likelihood estimators, class imbalance, cross validation, estimate bias/variance


Study Design
factorial designs, response surfaces, repeated measure designs, split-plot designs, case-control designs, use-availability designs, matched designs, crossover studies, probability surveys


Need to work on
reinforcement Learning, deep Neural Networks/deep Learning, natural language processing, image and computer vision
